source_propositions.source_text: H e uncorked a generation’s anger at a broken college entrance exam system.
Now the Gen Z movement that Abhijeet Dipke birthed five months ago and called the Cockroach Janta Party has become a formidable finger in the eye of the Indian government.
The cockroaches’ latest aim is the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner, over what they say is a politically motivated purge of 130 million voters from the election rolls.
Hundreds of protesters have been detained in Delhi during the latest demonstration by the Gen-Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) calling for electoral reforms.

The group said its founder Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - was detained with other leaders shortly after landing in Delhi.
Tens of thousands of security personnel were deployed and roads barricaded ahead of the demonstration, though the CJP insisted it would go ahead.
Delhi Police has not commented on the detentions, but had refused permission for the protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital.

The group - who are not registered as a political party in India - are seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections. It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has pulled out all the stops to prevent Cockroach movement protests taking over New Delhi.

They are here in support of the influential Gen-Z movement and Cockroach Janta Party, which have called for the resignation of India’s election chief, amid a bitter dispute over who gets to vote in the world’s most populous democracy.
Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms and a rollback of a controversial voter revision exercise which has struck 130 million names from the voter list.
For now, an eerie silence hangs over parts of central New Delhi.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government has gone to lengths to turn the city into a fortress, deploying nearly 30,000 personnel onto the streets.

source_propositions.source_text: Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.

Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.
But German police were already closing in on him.

After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.

Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".

Both he and his country have denied any involvement. It was 02:03 on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.
Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.
Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.
Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.
The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.

Prosecutors allege a yacht was used in the sabotage of pipelines, with the suspect leading the operation.

German federal prosecutors ⁠have filed charges ⁠against a 50-year-old Ukrainian national over a series of explosions that destroyed two Nord Stream underwater gas pipelines linking Russia to Europe in 2022.

The federal prosecutor’s office declined to comment on the specifics of the indictment on Wednesday against the accused, who is identified only as Serhii K in court documents under German privacy rules.
Serhii K is accused of attacking civilian energy infrastructure, causing an explosion, and destroying structures, according to the German public broadcaster ARD.

The underwater explosions damaged both the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 pipelines so severely that no gas could be transported through them, knocking out the key routes for Russian gas ⁠to Europe for months after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a December 2025 detention filing by the Federal Court of Justice, prosecutors allege that Serhii K helped coordinate a team that used a sailing yacht, the Andromeda, to place explosive devices on the pipelines near Denmark’s ⁠Bornholm Island in September 2022.

source_propositions.source_text: At least 12 people were killed and 309 others injured in an attack on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International airport in Riyadh as Iran-backed Houthis escalated the campaign they launched this summer against the kingdom.

The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said in a statement on Sunday that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed in the attack on late Saturday.
The authority said some of the injured were in critical condition and that all were receiving medical care at several hospitals.
Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter told Reuters.
Jordan's foreign ministry said in a statement on Saturday that two injured Jordanians were discharged from hospital while two others were still receiving treatment.
One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside.
More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing towards the facility.
An injured traveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.
All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
“We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the ⁠⁠⁠⁠recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said.

Israel’s acts of genocide and crimes against humanity , including forced displacement and extermination, have persisted throughout the ceasefire.
Other countries should take immediate measures to protect civilians and ensure that rights-based reconstruction begins.
The Board of Peace, authorized under United Nations Security Council Resolution 2803, is tasked with assessing parties’ compliance with the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict.
Promises of humanitarian relief and the restoration of essential civilian infrastructure are central to the plan.
Yet, a year on, aid volumes remain far below required levels , critical humanitarian access routes have been repeatedly obstructed, and reconstruction has not yet begun.

Continuing Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,400 Palestinians and wounded 4,881 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, bringing the death toll since October 2023 to over 74,000, including over 21,000 children.

“The outside world may be under a dangerous illusion that life in Gaza is returning to normal, but reality tells a very different story, ” said Sarah Sanbar , acting Israel and Palestine researcher at Human Rights Watch.
With winter approaching, families living in an Israel-engineered shelter crisis face preventable deaths and suffering affecting key human rights such as the rights to housing, health, and education.
Ninety-four percent of Gaza’s population lacks adequate shelter, the Palestine Shelter Cluster reported based on a survey of nearly 2,000 households across Gaza.
Nearly two-thirds of housing units have been destroyed , and many of those still standing are damaged and unsafe.

Humanitarian and human rights groups call out Israel’s continued killings and restrictions across the enclave.
One year after the so-called ceasefire in Gaza was reached with United States backing, it exists only on paper, according to more than 100 humanitarian, human rights and civil society organisations.

“The ceasefire exists in name only, with Israeli forces continuing to kill and injure Palestinians daily, and restrictions on aid, equipment and rebuilding materials preventing families from recovering,” a joint statement by the NGOs said on Friday.

Amnesty International, the Norwegian Refugee Council, Save the Children, Oxfam, Greenpeace and dozens of other international groups said Israeli attacks in the enclave have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians, including at least 327 children, in the year since US President Trump announced a deal to end hostilities as part of the Gaza Board of Peace framework.

“It is utterly shameful that a full year after the ceasefire was signed, so little has improved for Palestinians in Gaza,” Jan Egeland, secretary-general of the Norwegian Refugee Council, said in the joint statement.
Inger Ashing, chief executive of Save the Children, said, “A ceasefire is meaningless if children are still being killed and families are still unable to rebuild their lives.”

source_propositions.source_text: The top trade envoys for China and the European Union agreed Friday on a broad initial deal following two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over trade imbalances, the EU trade commissioner said.

Neither side provided clear details on the preliminary deal, but European Commissioner for Trade Maros Sefcovic said it includes lower tariffs for some European goods to China as well as measures to stabilize rare earth supply chains.
The EU trade envoy said the deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle imports to the EU and could lower tariffs on products benefiting “almost every” EU nation.
The deal would require approval from leaders across the 27-nation EU. He said that “by this step we are actually preventing several millions of car exports from China to the European Union.”
The two sides were seeking to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($403 billion) last year.
China’s Commerce Ministry posted online that Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao expressed concerns about the EU’s recent restrictive measures.

Sefcovic also said both sides reached understandings to further facilitate China’s export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets, as well as to improve access to the Chinese market for various EU products through lower most-favored-nation tariffs, including car parts, olive oil and footwear, totaling almost 4 billion euros (about $4.5 billion) in current export value.

The EU’s trade deficit with China widened to 103.3 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the second quarter, as imports rose to 153.6 billion euros ($172 billion), while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56 billion), according to EU statistics.
“As Europe’s largest economy, Germany welcomes foreign investment. At the same time, some investments can endanger the country’s security,” the German economic ministry said in a statement.
“The acquisition would have deepened dependencies and jeopardized the resilience of supply chains in Germany and the EU.”

Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.

Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.

The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.

“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.
China has been flooding Europe with cars , including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers.
Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery.
Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič says the agreement could prevent millions of Chinese vehicles from entering the European market over the next four years.
The European Union and China reached an agreement on Friday that will curb China’s booming hybrid car exports, delivering a breakthrough in negotiations aimed at rebalancing their trade relationship.

The announcement came as Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič wrapped up two days of talks in Beijing, the culmination of a push launched in June to narrow the bloc’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China.
The deal marks a win for the EU executive, which has been under pressure to secure concessions from Beijing.
Going into the talks, France and Germany strengthened Šefčovič’s hand by calling for the EU to take tough action on trade if China failed to curb a growing export glut.
Speaking in Beijing, the commissioner said the two sides had reached an agreement that would help to shield European automakers from low-price Chinese competition.

source_propositions.source_text: Ontario to begin removing Toronto bike lanes.
Here's what you need to know Ontario will begin removing bike lanes from a stretch on Bloor Street W. in Etobicoke on Tuesday, the Ministry of Transportation says.
A notice of construction start, issued by the ministry, says the work will occur on a 1.2-kilometre section between Clissold Road and Royal York Road.
Dakota Brasier, spokesperson for Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria, confirmed in an email on Thursday that bike lane removal will begin Oct.

"Following the ruling by the Ontario Court of Appeal, the province announced in September that it would immediately begin restoring motor vehicle lanes on Bloor Street West. That work begins Tuesday," Brasier said.
T he Court of Appeal ruled in August that Premier Doug Ford’s government could rip out 19 kilometres of protected bike lanes in Toronto, reversing a lower-court decision made in July 2025.
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said Thursday that the removal of the bike lanes is "completely unacceptable" and an affront to the city by Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

"That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city. Whether it is bike lanes, speed cameras, Island airport, every element we need to have our say. The city belong to all of us Torontonians through the municipal government," she said.

The ministry-issued notice says existing pavement markings and pre-cast concrete curbs will be removed and new pavement markings and signs "to safely restore" an additional vehicle lane in each direction will be installed.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow says of the bike lane removal: 'That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city.'

Michael Longfield, executive director of local cycling advocacy group CycleTO, said the organization is "outraged but not surprised" that the government has rejected the mayor's "win-win offer" to restore car lanes but keep bike lanes in Etobicoke.

"Ripping out these protected bike lanes against the will of Toronto city council is a colossal waste of $48 million. The province’s own experts know it will not ease traffic congestion, it will put people’s lives at risk, and there is no network of side streets that could replace these lanes."

source_propositions.source_text: Relentless monsoon rains, flash floods and landslides have left at least 44 people dead and affected more than one million people across seven districts in Bangladesh, authorities said on Sunday, as emergency responders continued relief operations amid warnings of further flooding.
According to the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, more than 1.022 million people have been affected by the flooding, with 267,918 families remaining stranded by rising waters.
At least 39 people have been injured since the severe weather began.

The worst-hit districts include Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar, Chattogram, Moulvibazar and Habiganj, where floodwaters have inundated 58 sub-districts (upazilas), damaging homes, roads, bridges and other critical infrastructure.
Although rainfall eased over the past 24 hours in several parts of the country, flood risks remain elevated.

The Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) warned that fresh short-term flooding could occur in Feni, Sylhet and northern districts, particularly along the Teesta River basin, due to continued upstream inflows and additional rainfall.
The agency said water levels at seven monitoring stations on the Sangu, Matamuhuri, Kushiyara, Manu and Someswari rivers remained above danger levels, keeping low-lying communities at risk.
Authorities have opened 1,131 emergency shelters, where 44,457 displaced people are currently staying after being evacuated from flood-affected areas.
The Disaster Management Ministry said it had allocated 145 million taka ($1.2 million) and 2,650 metric tonnes of rice to the seven worst-hit districts to support relief efforts.
Since July 7, district administrations across the country have also received 345 million taka and 6,900 metric tonnes of rice for emergency response operations.
(ILKHA) LEGAL WARNING: All rights of the published news, photos and videos are reserved by İlke Haber Ajansı Basın Yayın San.

Eight people, including two children, were killed in a mass shooting at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday, while the suspected gunman also died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, bringing the total death toll to nine, authorities said.

At least 44 people have died and more than 2,67,000 families have been affected as flooding ravaged seven districts across Bangladesh, according to the disaster management and relief ministry's latest situation report.
Authorities have opened 1,131 shelters, accommodating 44,457 displaced people.
Fifty-eight upazilas across seven districts – Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar, Chattogram, Moulvibazar and Habiganj – have been affected so far, disrupting normal life.
Flash floods and landslides caused by heavy rainfall have killed at least 43 people across five districts of Chattogram Division alone.

As of last night, water levels at seven monitoring stations on five rivers – Sangu and Matamuhuri rivers in Bandarban, Someswari in Netrokona, Kushiyara River in Sylhet, Manu River in Moulvibazar; and the Khowai River in Habiganj were above the danger level, according to Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) data.

Sardar Uday Raihan, executive engineer at the Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre, told The Business Standard that heavy to very heavy rainfall is forecast over the next 24 to 48 hours in parts of the Sylhet, Rangpur and Mymensingh divisions.

items.sourceTitle: Syria weighs military aid for Saudi Arabia amid Yemen war, sources say

source_propositions.source_text: RIYADH, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Syria is carefully considering providing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia amid an escalating war against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, a US official and a Syrian military official briefed on the matter said.

Options being considered include defensive aid to protect the kingdom from attacks, or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops fight the Houthis, the sources said.

The US official said Saudi Arabia had requested that Syria deploy forces to fight the Houthis - an assertion denied by the Syrian president's media adviser, Ahmad Zaidan, in a post on X following the publication of this story.

In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's civil war.

"Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries," the diplomat said in a statement.
The Saudi government media office and Yemen's information minister did not respond to requests for comment.

Saudi Arabia has been requesting assistance far and wide, from the US to Europe and the Middle East, for both defensive and offensive support in a renewed war against the group that follows weeks of Houthi missile and drone attacks on the kingdom.

items.sourceTitle: Codebreaker, 103, kept his WW2 heroics a secret for decades

source_propositions.source_text: Fred Vanke was sworn to secrecy but his work as a codebreaker has finally been recognised "My wife died and didn't know. I never told anybody. In fact, she always complained - all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell and you never tell anything."

From fleeing the Nazi invasion of his native Poland, to training as an operative to work behind enemy lines, to helping to crack the codes which turned the tide of the conflict, Fred Vanke had an eventful World War Two.
Sworn to secrecy however, his family and friends almost never learned of the true role the 103-year-old played in the Allied war effort.
But research into the life story of Vanke, now living in Breaston, Derbyshire, has written a new chapter on the history of Bletchley Park's famed codebreakers.
About 100 Poles based in the UK carried out work on behalf of Bletchley Park between 1940 and 1945.
After Fred shared his story, research has added the names of 27 Polish codebreakers and signals intelligence (sigint) to the Bletchley Park Roll of Honour, and more could follow.

The additions represent one of the most significant expansions of the documented Polish contribution to Britain's wartime codebreaking effort in recent years, helping historians better understand the scale of the intelligence partnership between Britain and the Polish government-in-exile.

That's the first time I've seen people being injured to that extent." Fred and his father served together in the Middle East After his initial destination Syria was lost with the invasion of France, he instead made his way to British-controlled Palestine where he joined the newly-formed Polish brigade, the Carpathian Rifle Brigade alongside his father. "I'm going to be a soldier at last," Fred remembers thinking. He proved his worth and after officer training in Tel Aviv he was sent to Glasgow to join the Cichociemni, a Polish special forces unit trained for occupied Poland. "Cichociemni in Polish means dark and quiet," he said. "I've gone right through the courses, how to use the poison, how to kill people quietly, and all that sort of thing.
"When I arrived there first, I never knew anybody there, it was a little strange, but very very soon it was like a holiday."

But I was very proud of Zygalski, Rejewski and Różycki - that's our three real codebreakers." Fred and Patricia met in Nottingham after the war After the war, Fred moved to Nottingham where he started a photography firm with a fellow Polish ex-paratrooper. "I met my wife in Jessops in one of the shops," he said. "She was a model there, once I saw her, I said 'this is my wife'." The couple raised three children, and were together until her death in 1996 - but Fred never told her about his wartime role. "My wife died and she still didn't know what I was doing.
"The evidence proving direct links to Bletchley Park and other secret intelligence work is truly important and shows the depth of our co-operation, which needs to be recognised."

As war rages inside Sudan and the humanitarian aid network nears collapse, millions of refugees both inside the country and in neighbouring nations are losing hope they will ever be able to return home safely.
Instead, they fight for survival in isolated refugee camps, which are bursting at the seams.
The Independent visited four Sudanese refugee camps in eastern Chad, where more than one million Sudanese refugees currently reside in isolated desert camps.
Inside a 6m² shelter in the Goudrane Camp in Chad, a baby born in the battle for the city of El Fasher in western Sudan, wriggles on the carpet.
Inside the tarpaulin walls, his mother, Maymauna, 27, cushions the back of her son’s head.

Families also recount how they were specifically targeted and massacred by RSF soldiers, a predominantly Arab group, because they were members of the Masalit tribe, one of the largest ethnic African tribes in western Sudan before the war.
Human rights investigators have since called attacks initiated by the RSF and allied Arab militias examples of ethnic cleansing, while the United Nations found ‘hallmarks of genocide’ in El Fasher.
“For them, suffocation stops the slower, more painful death from thirst and starvation.”
But last month, despite digging more than 128 metres deep into the Goudrane camp’s dusty ground, no water was found in the east part of the camp.
“We need to create long-term solutions quickly because the need right now is so great in the camps.”

As the war in Sudan pushes more people across the border, malnutrition is on the rise in Chad’s remote settlements where 86% of the refugees are women and children F or hours, jolting along the waterlogged dirt track to the hospital, 18-year-old Makka Ibraheem Mohammed held on tight to her seat and focused on stopping herself vomiting. She was in labour, in extreme pain after her uterus ruptured, but was now being tossed around in the ambulance that jumped along the dips and bumps of the road through the Chadian desert.

Most of the 878,000 Sudanese refugees who have fled to Chad since 2023, living hand to mouth in this harsh landscape, are women. They stay in isolated camps in the desert with limited water and food, no work and with medical help often a life-threateningly long distance away.
The hospital Mohammed needed, run by the aid agency Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), was in Metche, another refugee camp more than two hours away.

“I kept getting infections during my pregnancy and I had to go the clinic seven times – when I was there, the pregnancy started. But I wasn’t able to give birth normally because my uterus had collapsed,” says Mohammed.

items.sourceTitle: Seaweed Farming on a Madagascar Island Balances Livelihoods and Lagoon

source_propositions.source_text: On the small island of Nosy Boraha, off Madagascar's northeastern coast, an unusual agricultural boom is unfolding beneath the surface of a shallow turquoise lagoon.
Farmers wade through water barely five meters deep, tying fragments of a reddish seaweed known locally as cottonii to lines anchored in the sand.
The crop, Kappaphycus alvarezii, is prized worldwide as a source of carrageenan, a gelling agent that ends up in everything from ice cream to toothpaste.

As wild fish stocks around the island decline, seaweed farming has emerged as a vital supplementary income for villagers such as those of Ilampy, and it has been folded into Madagascar's national blue economy strategy as a flagship of sustainable coastal development.

Yet a new interdisciplinary study published in PLOS Sustainability and Transformation suggests that the story of this booming aquaculture is far more intricate than a simple success narrative, weaving together ecology, anthropology, and environmental law in a single portrait of a lagoon under change.

The research, led by Isabel Urbina-Barreto of the IRD and colleagues including Rindra Razandriarison, Aline Tribollet, and a team spanning French and Malagasy institutions, set out in 2024 to answer questions that most single-discipline studies leave unasked.
What does seaweed cultivation actually do to the benthic habitats of a tropical lagoon?

This kind of triangulation is rare in aquaculture research, where environmental monitoring and social science often proceed on separate tracks, and it allowed the researchers to see connections that would otherwise remain invisible.

Within the zones used for seaweed cultivation, the ecologists identified four genera of seagrass and three genera of macroalgae, while coral communities, made up of approximately four genera, were found mainly concentrated near the reef crest, at some distance from the main farming areas.
The scale of cultivation is more modest than the headline numbers might suggest.

The company Nosy Boraha Seaweed holds rights to operate across about 300 hectares of the lagoon, an area that sounds enormous until one learns that the actual cultivation plots cover only 8.3 percent of that concession.
Whether that expansion proceeds without degrading the lagoon will depend on the environmental safeguards that accompany it, a question the study addresses directly.

Seaweed has become a key cash crop as climate change and industrial trawling test the resilient culture of the semi-nomadic Vezo people A long Madagascar’s south-west coast, the Vezo people, who have fished the Mozambique Channel for countless generations, are defined by a way of life sustained by the sea.
Yet climate change and industrial exploitation are pushing this ocean-based culture to its limits.
Coastal villages around Toliara, a city in southern Madagascar, host tens of thousands of the semi-nomadic Vezo people , who make a living from small-scale fishing on the ocean.
For centuries, they have launched pirogues , small boats carved from single tree trunks, every day into the turquoise shallows to catch tuna, barracuda and grouper.
“We rely solely on the ocean,” says Soa Nomeny, a woman from a small island off the south-west coast called Nosy Ve.
“Whatever we catch today, we eat today. If we catch nothing, we don’t eat.”

items.sourceTitle: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft

source_propositions.source_text: Lucknow brides can no longer afford traditional silver nagras In Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh and a city known for its Nawabi heritage and artisanship, 55-year-old Azhar Hussain sits at the bench where he has spent years making decorative footwear. His tools are still there, but the customers are not.
Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted.
The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts.

For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras. He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal.
Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place.

“Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842.
Globally, silver currently costs $2,100 (201,000 rupees) per kg, but in India, it’s more than 20 percent higher because of heavy government import taxes and strict licensing that chokes off supply.
India depends on imports to meet more than 80% of its domestic silver demand and its purchases account for over 20 percent of the global trade in refined silver.
That saw silver imports plunge by 87 percent to just $75.6 million that month, down from $566.2 million the previous year, the country’s lowest level in over three years.

“I don’t know what our future looks like anymore. Sometimes I think about what will happen to this craft and I cry. This wasn’t just our profession; it was our identity, our heritage and everything we were known for.”

items.sourceTitle: Drone-sprayed bear repellent undergoes testing in northeastern Japan city - The Mainichi

source_propositions.source_text: Please view the main text area of the page by skipping the main menu.

KITAAKITA, Akita -- A nonprofit group has started spraying a bear repellent by drone in this northeastern Japan city as part of a demonstration experiment set to continue until around the time bears enter hibernation.
The Center of Historical Materials for Science in Akita, a nonprofit group based in Odate, Akita Prefecture, developed the repellent using wood vinegar.
The organization, known as Kemusa, works to promote a deeper understanding of the region's natural environment.

On Oct. 2, the repellent was sprayed from the air over an apple orchard in Kitaakita as more than 40 students from the neighboring Takanosu campus of Akita Prefectural Hinai special needs school, along with other people involved, looked on.
"By adding repellent spraying to bear countermeasures, we may be able to achieve even greater effectiveness," said Kazuhiro Sato, 72, chairperson of the organization.
The wood vinegar contained in the repellent is a naturally derived liquid collected by cooling smoke produced during charcoal production.

In recent years, bears have been spotted near homes in urban areas and mountain communities in Kitaakita, as well as in fields along roadsides, with crop damage and human injuries occurring one after another.
The municipal government has implemented measures such as clearing grass and undergrowth in forests, installing electric fences and cutting down unmanaged fruit trees.

items.sourceTitle: The Man Behind a West Bank Telegram Channel Trying to Keep Palestinian Drivers Safe

source_propositions.source_text: At 30, Hattab’s life now revolves around these checkpoints—perhaps more than any other Palestinian in the occupied West Bank.

But he has also transformed his community’s approach to them: Nearly 350,000 people follow his traffic Telegram group, which has closed a gap left open by major navigation apps that fail Palestinian users.
Local radio stations build their hourly road segments off his dispatches.
A routing system used by West Bank companies and a new local app pull his data into their own.
Hattab was working during the day as a digital designer at a newspaper in Ramallah.
When one shift ended, he started another, this time as the paper’s delivery driver.

That meant that most nights, Hattab had to drive all around the West Bank. He found himself dodging Israeli military raids, settlements he had to route around and, most of all, unpredictable checkpoints, which could cause hours-long delays and where armed Israeli soldiers could search him or his car.

A Palestinian driver who follows their directions risks being arrested, fined, or shot. They came in a trickle, at first, and then, as checkpoints began to multiply in 2022 and delays got worse, they came in a flood.

An investigation we published in September, in partnership with the Palestine Reporting Lab, Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism, and Lighthouse Reports, found that checkpoint delays have increased by more than 50 percent since then.
Our analysis found that the average commuter in the West Bank now loses about 77 hours every year taking roundabout routes to avoid checkpoints.

source_propositions.source_text: A Mi'kmaw community in Cape Breton is placing a big bet on new technology that it says can turn seawater into environmentally friendly jet fuel.

Eskasoni First Nation has invested $1.5 million and is the majority owner in a joint venture called eFuels Mi'kmaq Limited that plans to build a pilot project on band-owned land in Cape Breton Regional Municipality's industrial park in Sydney harbour.

Bertram Bernard, a band councillor and chair of Eskasoni Corporate Services, said the investment will create local jobs for band members and is an important step in taking a meaningful role in a growing industry.

"For us, this is about creating long-term economic opportunities, while continuing to be responsible stewards of our land and waters," he said during an announcement Thursday at the Sarah Denny Cultural Centre in Eskasoni.

The newly formed eFuels Mi'kmaq plans to extract hydrogen from seawater and draw carbon dioxide from the air to create what is known as drop-in fuel, meaning it can be burned like any other fuel without any engine modifications.
The process is expected to be powered by wind energy from onshore and offshore sources as they become available.
Eskasoni band councillor Bertram Bernard says the joint venture will create lasting economic benefits while ensuring stewardship of resources.

source_propositions.source_text: Fishermen at Dixcove have rejected GoldCoast Resource Corporation's bid to explore for gold offshore, saying the ocean that sustains their families cannot be handed over without their consent.
For generations, the waters off Dixcove in the Ahanta West Municipality have put food on tables and paid school fees for families along Ghana's Western Region coastline.
Now, fishermen there say that lifeline is under threat from a proposed offshore gold exploration project they were never properly consulted about.

Fishermen in the coastal town have rejected plans by GoldCoast Resource Corporation to explore for gold offshore, arguing the venture could endanger their livelihoods and damage the marine environment, according to the Ghanaian Times .

The fishermen insist the ocean remains their traditional source of food and income, and that any decision affecting its use must involve the communities whose survival depends on it. Their position emerged on Tuesday during an engagement organised by Friends of the Nation (FON), a civil society organisation that works on coastal and marine conservation issues, the Ghanaian Times reports.
The meeting brought together stakeholders at Dixcove to discuss the proposed exploration and examine its possible effects on fishing grounds, marine ecosystems and the wider coastal economy.

According to the newspaper, the engagement was designed to promote the protection of Ghana's ocean resources, uphold the rights of fishermen, and safeguard the sustainability of livelihoods along the coast.

Any disruption to fishing grounds — whether through exploration activity, pollution, or restricted access to the sea — could ripple through household incomes, local fish markets, and food security in communities that have few alternative sources of livelihood.

Friends of the Nation's continued engagement with coastal stakeholders suggests the organisation intends to keep pressing the issue, but no specific dates for further action, hearings, or government responses have been disclosed.

08, GNA – Friends of the Nation (FoN), a non-government organisation (NGO), has declared zero tolerance for mining activities in the ocean as part of its efforts to ensure justice in fisheries governance.

The declaration followed government’s proposed offshore gold reconnaissance deal, granting 10 contiguous offshore reconnaissance licences to Gold Coast Resources Ghana Limited to undertake gold mining in Ghana’s marine waters from Half-Assini in Jomoro to Winneba in the Effutu Municipality in the Western and Central Regions.
According to the NGO, gold mining in the high seas would disrupt the activities of artisanal fishers, thereby bringing fishing expeditions to a standstill.

Mr Mevuta Donkris, the Executive Director of the FoN, said this at a day’s workshop for stakeholders in the fishing industry at Dixcove in the Ahanta West Municipality of the Western Region. It was organised by FoN under the project dubbed “Protecting Our Zone, Securing Our Future” and was attended by chief fishermen and women from Lower and Upper Dixcove, canoe owners, fish mongers, fishers, the Fisheries Commission, FoN and the media.
The Minerals Commission has suspended the Reconnaissance License of Gold Coast GRC Ghana Limited.
A letter intercepted by Myjoyonline indicates that the decision to suspend the license is part of the mining sector clean-up being carried out by the regulator.

Minister for Lands and Natural Resources has directed the immediate suspension of all activities being undertaken under the licences." It said, "The suspension shall remain in effect until the Commission has completed the necessary consultations and issued the requisite written Ministerial authorisation for the resumption of activities.

During this period, the company is required to cooperate fully with the Commission, other relevant State institutions and all affected stakeholders in addressing the concerns raised and ensuring that all applicable regulatory, environmental and social requirements are duly satisfied.

Seventeen years ago, a char emerged in Purba Naodoba union of Zajira upazila in Shariatpur.
On it grew a village called Alam Kha Kandi, and in 2017, the No 122 Altaf Hossain Khan Government Primary School was built there on 33 decimals of land.
Back then, the Padma river was nearly two kilometres away -- not visible from the school gate.
That distance has been vanishing.
Over the past two years, successive bouts of erosion have dragged the river steadily closer, and it now licks at the school's own grounds, just 50 metres from the building.
Teachers, students and local residents fear what has already happened twice nearby -- in 2024 and 2025, two primary schools in neighbouring villages of the same union were lost to the river.
On a recent visit, the national flag still stood tall outside the erosion-battered school on the Padma's bank.
Erosion anxiety follows the students constantly, teachers said, and with the school itself at risk, safety concerns run alongside the lessons.
"The river keeps eroding and has come right onto our school field," said Borna Akter, a fourth-grade student, speaking to The Daily Star.

"Our school could break apart at any time. It feels very scary, wondering when our school will break down. If our school goes into the river, we won't be able to study here anymore. Where will we study then? We want arrangements made to protect our school."
School teacher Naimur Rahman Khan said panic over the erosion alone had already driven at least 100 students away.

source_propositions.source_text: More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds.
In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age.
Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered.
Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified.

We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time.
The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times.
We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth.

These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy.

The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found.

Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies.

First discovered in 2007, fast radio bursts are enigmatic, millisecond-long flashes of radio emission from the distant universe. Their origin remains uncertain, particularly since most are seen once and never again.

Astronomers using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope have pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) seen to date. Their finding has implications for what kind of energetic event creates these bursts.

“What makes fast radio bursts interesting is that we don't know what generates them. We have theories for what objects produce them, but we don't have conclusive proof,” said Manisha Caleb of the University of Sydney, lead author on the study published Thursday in the journal Science.
The MeerTRAP team used the MeerKAT telescope to detect the burst on March 4, 2024, leading to its designation as FRB 20240304B.
Record breaker dates back to just 3 billion years after the big bang.

Astronomers using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope have discovered and precisely localized the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded, a powerful flash of radio waves lasting only a few milliseconds that travelled for more than 10 billion years across the cosmos before reaching Earth.
FRBs are enigmatic objects whose brief radio flashes are detectable half-way across the universe.
First identified in 2007, their origins remain uncertain, particularly since most are seen only once.
The research reported today started with the discovery by the MeerTRAP team of a radio burst on March 4, 2024, leading to its designation as FRB 20240304B.
The MeerKAT data precisely localized the FRB and suggested that it was extremely distant, but to measure the distance accurately astronomers would need to study its host galaxy.

source_propositions.source_text: A royal archive unearthed at the ancient Hittite settlement of Samuha, in present-day Sivas in central Türkiye, has shed new light on the Hittite Empire , revealing records of a deadly epidemic, military threats and royal life dating back about 3,400 years.
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced that archaeologists uncovered 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments during the 2026 excavations at Kayalıpınar in Sivas’ Yıldızeli district.
Together with 53 tablets and fragments found at the site last year, the number of discoveries has reached 184.
The documents, dating to the reign of King Tudhaliya II, are considered the most extensive Hittite-language archive discovered in the 21st century, according to the excavation team.
The ancient settlement is known as Samuha in Assyrian and Hittite sources.
The tablets, written in Hittite and Hurrian, provide firsthand records of state administration, military affairs, religious practices and the experiences of the royal family.
“The royal archive at Kayalıpınar has taken its place in history as the most comprehensive Hittite-language archive uncovered in the 21st century,” Ersoy said in a statement shared on social media.
Another tablet records her death and the funeral rites performed for her.
The archive also contains evidence of the military pressures facing the Hittite state.
The generals warned that the Hittite army could be destroyed if the requested reinforcements failed to arrive.
The newly discovered texts also offer insight into Hittite divination practices, particularly the use of birds to interpret omens.

The archive includes texts covering divination, correspondence, rituals and prayers, offering researchers new material for studying Hittite religious practices as well as the development of the Hittite language and scribal culture.
